title: Getting started
description: Start, automate, continue, and resume a session.

pages.text:
Starting Claude Code
Start a normal interactive session
TERMINAL
claude
Then, ask it do anything,
→ Explore this project and explain how product data currently flows from the database
to the storefront.
Start Claude with the first task already provided
claude "your task"
Example,
claude "find out why the inventory tests are failing"
Useful when you already know exactly what you want Claude to start with.

Run one task and exit
claude -p "your task"
Example,
claude -p "review the current git diff for obvious regressions"
Claude performs the task, outputs the result, and exits.
USE IT WHEN
You want Claude inside:
shell scripts CI pipelines
automated checks cron jobs
command pipelines other developer tools
You can pipe information into it too:
tail -n 300 app.log | claude -p "find the likely cause of these errors"

Continue your latest session
claude -c
Use this when you closed Claude Code but want to continue the most recent conversation in
the current project.
Resume a specific older session
claude -r
or:
claude -r "auth-refactor"
Inside Claude Code:
/resume
Use this when you want to return to a particular piece of work instead of starting fresh.
Claude Code stores sessions separately, and resuming continues the existing session
rather than copying it.

description: Your everyday command reference.

pages.text:
The Commands You'll Use Constantly

you
You forget a command

context
Moving to unrelated work
/compact Compresses current
conversation
Same task, context getting large

used
Claude starts losing track

instructions
You want to see what Claude
remembers

level
/effort Change reasoning effort Hard debugging or architecture
/permissions Manage what Claude can do Control access/actions
/plan Enter Plan Mode Approach needs review first

COMMAND WHAT IT DOES USE IT WHEN

immediately editing
Before merging

Anthropic's current command reference groups these around setup, active development,

title: Clear, compact, or branch?
description: Choose the right way to manage a conversation.

pages.text:
/clear vs /compact vs /branch
These solve three different problems.
/clear
Different problem
/compact
Same problem + too much
context
/branch
Try another approach
safely
/clear
USE IT WHEN
You're moving from one unrelated task to another.
EXAMPLE
You just spent 40 minutes debugging authentication. Now you want to redesign the
product page.
Run /clear because all that authentication context probably isn't useful anymore.
/compact
USE IT WHEN
You're still working on the same problem, but the session has become large.
You can tell Claude what matters:

/compact preserve all database schema decisions, migration problems and
unresolved inventory issues
So:
Same problem + too much context = /compact
Different problem = /clear
/branch try-different-schema
This creates another conversation from the current point while leaving the original intact.
USE IT WHEN
You want to experiment with another direction without destroying the path you're
already on.
EXAMPLE
You've spent an hour designing inventory around:
CURRENT PATH
stock stored directly on Product
BRANCH
a separate inventory table
but you want to see whether a separate inventory table would be cleaner.
Instead of derailing your current conversation:
/branch inventory-table-experiment
Then explore the alternative there. You can later resume the original session.

title: Forking a conversation
description: Explore inherited context and background side tasks.

pages.text:
/fork
This one deserves its own explanation because its behavior has changed.
In standard Claude Code behavior, /fork can act as an alias for /branch .
That means:
/fork experimental-checkout
can branch the current conversation.
FORKED SUBAGENT BEHAVIOR
Claude Code also has a newer forked subagent behavior. When that functionality is
enabled, /fork can instead launch another agent that inherits the current
conversation context and works in the background.
EXAMPLE
/fork draft unit tests for the parser changes so far
You can keep working in the main conversation while the fork handles that side task.
This is different from a normal subagent because a normal subagent starts with a focused
context supplied by the parent, while a fork can inherit the current conversation history.
NORMAL SUBAGENT
starts with a focused context supplied
by the parent
FORK
can inherit the current conversation
history

USE FORK WHEN
The side task needs to understand a lot of what has already happened in the
current conversation.
EXAMPLE
MAIN AGENT Implementing checkout.
FORK /fork review everything we've decided about checkout so
far and identify edge cases we haven't covered
Meanwhile, you keep implementing.

title: Context management
description: Keep the right information in focus.

pages.text:
Context Management
Claude doesn't only carry your messages.
The context window can contain:
conversation history tool results
files Claude read CLAUDE.md
terminal output memory
loaded Skills MCP results
information returned from subagents
That means context quality matters.

/context
Use it when Claude seems to be:
forgetting instructions
repeating itself
referencing stale decisions
becoming less focused
carrying too much irrelevant information
Think of /context as:
What's currently taking up Claude's attention?
/btw
For a small side question:
/btw Why did you use a composite index here?
This is useful when you want an answer without adding that entire tangent to your main
conversation history.

title: Project guidance: CLAUDE.md
description: Give every session a useful starting point.

pages.text:
CLAUDE.md
CLAUDE.md is persistent project guidance Claude can load when working in
your project.
A project-level file might contain:
CLAUDE.MD PROJECT LEVEL
# Commands
- Package manager: pnpm
- Dev server: `pnpm dev`
- Typecheck: `pnpm typecheck`
- Tests: `pnpm test`
# Database
- Use Drizzle ORM for database access
- Schema lives inside `src/db/schema/`
- Never manually modify generated migration files
# Frontend
- Reuse existing UI primitives before creating new ones
- Follow the established spacing and typography tokens

/init
/init
Claude inspects the repository and creates or improves a starting CLAUDE.md .
USE IT WHEN
You open Claude Code inside:
an existing repository a project you didn't build
a legacy app a monorepo
a new project that has started developing conventions
Don't blindly keep everything Claude generates.
Review it.

title: Where instructions belong
description: Match each instruction to the right control.

pages.text:
Where Instructions Should Live
A simple rule:
Something Claude should always know → CLAUDE.md
A repeatable way of doing work → Skill
Something that MUST happen → Hook
Something Claude must not be allowed to do → Permissions
A one-time request → Prompt
External service or tool → MCP
Separate focused investigation → Subagent
This distinction becomes very important as your setup grows.

title: Permissions
description: Configure allow, ask, and deny rules.

pages.text:
Permissions
Claude Code isn't just producing text.
It can actually:
Read Write Edit Run Bash Use Git Call MCP tools
Access external services
Permissions control which of those actions are allowed.
Open them using:
/permissions
The core rule groups are:
allow ask deny

EXAMPLE
SETTINGS
{
"permissions": {
"allow": [
"Bash(pnpm typecheck)",
"Bash(pnpm test *)",
"Bash(git status)",
"Bash(git diff *)"
],
"ask": [
"Bash(git push *)"
],
"deny": [
"Read(.env)",
"Read(.env.*)",
"Edit(.env)",
"Edit(.env.*)"
]
}
}
Good use
LET CLAUDE FREELY RUN
pnpm typecheck
 pnpm test
 git status
BUT ASK BEFORE
git push
AND PREVENT DIRECT ACCESS TO
.env

title: Permission modes
description: Understand the mode you are working in.

pages.text:
Permission Modes
Press:
Shift + Tab
to cycle between available modes.
You'll commonly work with:
Manual Claude asks more often.
Good while learning or working somewhere sensitive.
Accept Edits Normal edits become less annoying to approve.
Useful once you're comfortable with the task.
Plan Claude investigates and proposes first.
Auto Claude Code uses its safety system to decide whether many
actions can proceed automatically.
Always look at the current mode rather than assuming you're in the same mode as
someone else's tutorial.

title: Plan before implementing
description: Investigate the approach before changing code.

pages.text:
Plan Mode
Enter it with:
/plan
EXAMPLE
/plan Replace the current local product data with PostgreSQL using
Drizzle. Study how products are currently consumed before deciding the
schema. We only need categories, products and stock right now.
Plan Mode is for:
01
Think first.
02
Inspect first.
03
Don't jump
straight into
implementation.
Claude can explore the project and form an implementation approach before you approve
normal source edits.

Good tasks for Plan Mode
Use it for:
database changes authentication
permissions architecture
migration work large refactors
unfamiliar code features spanning several systems
decisions that are expensive to reverse
Usually skip it for
Change this text Fix this margin
Rename this variable Add an icon

EXAMPLE
BAD Build product variants.
BETTER
/plan Study the current product and inventory implementation and
propose how product variants should be introduced without breaking
existing products. Include schema changes, migration path, API impact,
admin changes and storefront changes. Don't implement yet.
Then challenge the plan:
→ Why do we need a separate inventory table?
→ Can this first version avoid variant-level pricing?
→ What existing code will break if we do it this way?
That conversation can save you from reviewing a terrible
2,000-line diff later.

description: Match capability to the work.

pages.text:
Models

Faster model

Renaming
Formatting

title: Reasoning effort
description: Choose how deeply to reason about a task.

pages.text:
Effort
Use:
/effort
or:
/effort high
Think about model and effort separately.
Model
which brain you're using
Effort
how hard you want it to think on this
task
DON'T USE MAXIMUM EFFORT FOR
Change button text to "Checkout"
USE HIGHER EFFORT FOR
Figure out why checkout occasionally creates duplicate orders under
concurrent requests.

title: Reusable skills
description: Package a repeatable development process.

pages.text:
Skills
A Skill is a reusable process Claude can follow.
Project Skills live inside:
.claude/skills/
EXAMPLE
PROJECT STRUCTURE
.claude/
skills/
build-ui/
SKILL.md

Example /build-ui
SKILL.MD
---
description: Build or significantly update customer-facing UI
using the existing project's components, design system and re
sponsive patterns.
---
Build:
$ARGUMENTS
BEFORE IMPLEMENTING
1. Inspect the existing page.
2. Search for reusable
components.
3. Inspect the design
tokens.
4. Check how similar pages
are structured.
DURING IMPLEMENTATION
1. Reuse existing primitives.
2. Keep the change
focused.
3. Follow established
typography and spacing.
4. Make it responsive.
BEFORE FINISHING
1. Run the application.
2. Inspect the result.
3. Run typecheck.
4. Report what changed.
Now:
/build-ui create the New Arrivals page

title: When to create a skill
description: Recognize workflows worth saving.

pages.text:
When to Create a Skill
If you catch yourself repeatedly typing something like:
First inspect this.
Then check that.
Then follow these conventions.
Then test these things.
Then report using this structure.
that's probably a Skill.
Useful examples:
/build-ui
 /review-ui
 /build-feature
 /verify-feature
/review-changes
 /debug
 /deploy

title: Dynamic skills
description: Include live command output in a workflow.

pages.text:
Dynamic Skills
Skills can include live command output.
EXAMPLE
SKILL.MD
## Current Diff!`git diff HEAD`
Review these changes for:
- bugs
- regressions
- unnecessary changes
- missing tests
- violations of CLAUDE.md
Then:
/review-changes
automatically reviews whatever currently changed.
No copying the diff manually.

title: Subagents
description: Delegate a focused investigation with separate context.

pages.text:
Subagents
A subagent is another Claude worker with its own context.
The important part isn't that it's an “AI expert.”
The important part is:
01
Separate context.
02
Focused task.
03
Useful result
returned to the
main agent.

Good use
Suppose you're implementing inventory management.
The main Claude could delegate:
MAIN CLAUDE
Agent 1 → inspect database and stock model
Agent 2 → inspect admin product editing flow
Agent 3 → inspect test coverage and edge cases
Each agent can read lots of files.
 The main conversation only needs
their findings.

/agents
Current Claude Code docs again show /agents as the interface for managing
subagents, including active agents and reusable agent configurations. Older Claude
Code versions changed this behavior several times, so if an older tutorial says
/agents disappeared, check your current version.
Custom subagent
Create:
.claude/agents/feature-reviewer.md
EXAMPLE
FEATURE-REVIEWER.MD
---
name: feature-reviewer
description: Review a completed feature in a fresh context fo
r bugs, regressions, unnecessary changes and missing verifica
tion.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
Review the requested feature.
Return:
## Critical## Major## Minor## Verification## Recommendation

title: Background tasks
description: Inspect work running inside a session.

pages.text:
Then:
→ Use the feature-reviewer agent to independently review the inventory feature.
Custom agents can also control things such as model, effort, permissions, Skills, MCP servers,
background execution and worktree isolation.
17
/tasks
/tasks
Shows work currently running in the background of this session.
Use it when:
Claude started subagents. A Bash command is still running.
A fork is working. Something has been backgrounded.
You can inspect and manage those running tasks from there.

title: Background sessions
description: Keep a full session working after detaching.

pages.text:
/background
This is where Claude Code gets much more interesting.
Run:
 /background or:
 /bg
to detach the current Claude session and let it continue working without keeping your
terminal occupied.
You can also give it one last instruction:
/bg run the full test suite and fix any failures
Claude keeps working in the background.
You can then manage those sessions using:
claude agents
Anthropic's current CLI also lets you start directly in the background:
claude --bg "investigate the flaky checkout test"
And later:
claude attach <id>
claude logs <id>
claude stop <id>

title: Agent View
description: Monitor multiple background sessions.

pages.text:
Agent View
Run:
claude agents
This gives you a screen where you can see multiple background Claude sessions and which
ones are working, need input, finished, failed.
This is different from:
/agents
Think of them like this:
/agents
→ agents inside the current Claude
workflow
claude agents
→ dashboard for multiple full Claude
sessions
Anthropic currently describes Agent View as a research preview.

title: Git worktrees
description: Give parallel work an isolated checkout.

pages.text:
Git Worktrees
If two agents are editing the same checkout at once, you can get conflicts fast.
Worktrees solve the filesystem side of that problem.
Start Claude inside an isolated worktree:
claude --worktree feature-auth
or:
claude -w feature-auth
Claude creates an isolated checkout under:
.claude/worktrees/
by default.
EXAMPLE
TERMINAL 1
claude -w inventory
TERMINAL 2
claude -w checkout
TERMINAL 3
claude -w admin-
dashboard
Now three Claude sessions can work without directly editing the same filesystem checkout.

title: Worktrees and subagents
description: Combine filesystem and context isolation.

pages.text:
Worktree vs Subagent
These solve different problems.
Subagent
→ context isolation
Worktree
→ filesystem isolation
You can combine both.
A custom agent can include:
isolation: worktree
Then whenever that subagent changes code, it gets its own isolated checkout.

title: Batch changes
description: Split large, separable migrations into units.

pages.text:
/batch
This is for big changes.
EXAMPLE
/batch migrate src/ from Solid to React
Claude first researches the codebase and breaks the job into independent units.
01 Claude researches the codebase
02 splits a large change into roughly 5-30 independent pieces
03 you approve the plan
04 units are handed to background subagents in isolated worktrees
05 each unit can implement, test, and open a pull request
Current Anthropic docs say /batch can split a large change into roughly 5-30
independent pieces. After you approve the plan, those units are handed to background
subagents in isolated worktrees, and each unit can implement, test, and open a
pull request.

Good /batch tasks
/batch migrate all Jest tests to Vitest
/batch replace deprecated API client usage across packages
/batch move all legacy React class components in src/ to functional
components
/batch update every package in this monorepo to the new logging API
These are large, divisible changes.
Bad /batch tasks
/batch build checkout
Checkout may involve tightly coupled decisions.
Not every large feature can safely be sliced into independent PRs.
Use /batch when the work is genuinely separable.

title: MCP integrations
description: Connect external tools and data.

pages.text:
MCP
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.
It lets Claude connect to tools and systems outside your local codebase.
THINK
GitHub Jira Sentry Notion Databases
Internal APIs Monitoring systems Custom business tools
Anthropic's MCP docs recommend using MCP when you find yourself repeatedly
copying information from another service into Claude manually.

Add an MCP server
EXAMPLE
claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
LIST SERVERS claude mcp list
INSPECT ONE claude mcp get notion
REMOVE ONE claude mcp remove notion
Inside Claude Code:
/mcp
opens the MCP manager and can also handle authentication for supported remote servers.

title: Hooks
description: Run automatic actions on lifecycle events.

pages.text:
Hooks
A SKILL SAYS
Claude should follow this workflow.
A HOOK SAYS
This action runs automatically when
this event happens.
That's a major difference.
Anthropic describes hooks as deterministic automation tied to events in Claude
Code's lifecycle.
/hooks
/hooks
opens the configured hooks browser.
Current versions treat this mainly as an inspection interface. You configure hooks in settings
files or ask Claude to create them.

title: Formatting hook example
description: Automate formatting after file edits.

title: Blocking commands with hooks
description: Inspect commands before they run.

pages.text:
Hook Example: Block
Dangerous Commands
Use:
PreToolUse
before Bash commands.
Your script can inspect the command and reject things such as:
rm -rf /
DROP DATABASE
git push --force
This is stronger than adding:
Don't run dangerous commands.
to a prompt.

title: Hook events
description: Find the lifecycle event for your automation.

pages.text:
Important Hook Events
Useful ones include:
SessionStart TeammateIdle
UserPromptSubmit PreCompact
PreToolUse PostCompact
PostToolUse WorktreeCreate
Notification WorktreeRemove
SubagentStart Stop
SubagentStop SessionEnd
TaskCreated
TaskCompleted
Current Claude Code exposes many lifecycle events, including specific events for
subagents, agent teams, tasks, and worktrees.

title: Engineering controls compared
description: Understand the boundaries between the tools.

pages.text:
Skills vs Hooks vs MCP vs Subagents
This is worth remembering:
CLAUDE.md → permanent project context
Skills → repeatable way of doing work
Hooks → something that should happen automatically
MCP → connection to another system
Subagents → isolated delegated work
Worktrees → isolated files
Agent teams → multiple agents coordinating together

Mention Files Directly
Instead of:
Look somewhere in the authentication code.
you can say:

Or:

Useful when you already know what matters.
35
Shell Commands

title: Troubleshooting
description: Diagnose installation and environment issues.

pages.text:
/doctor
If Claude Code behaves strangely:
/doctor
or:
claude doctor
Use it for:
Installation problems Hook problems
Broken settings Plugin problems
MCP issues Environment issues

title: Everyday workflow
description: A practical path from feature request to review.

pages.text:
A Practical Everyday Workflow
For a normal feature:
01 Start Claude
02 Make sure project context is correct
03 Give it one focused feature
04 Use /plan if the approach matters
05 Review the plan
06 Implement
07 Watch what files and commands Claude uses
08 Let Claude verify the result
09 /diff
10 Run tests
11 Use a fresh subagent or /review for important changes
12 /security-review when appropriate
13 Update CLAUDE.md if a permanent project rule changed
14 /compact if you're continuing the same work
15 /clear before unrelated work

title: The mental model
description: Combine controls around the work you need done.

pages.text:
ONE MENTAL MODEL TO REMEMBER
You don't get better results from Claude
Code by memorizing more commands. You
get better results by knowing which
problem you're trying to solve.
Need context?
→  CLAUDE.md
Need isolated files?
→  Worktree
Need a repeatable process?
→  Skill
Need coordinated workers?
→  Agent Team
Need a guaranteed action?
→  Hook
Need large-scale parallel work?
→  /batch
Need an external system?
→  MCP
Need Claude working while you move on?
→  /background
Need isolated thinking?
→  Subagent
Need to review the approach first?
→  /plan
Need to recover from a mistake?
→  /rewind
Once you understand those boundaries, Claude Code stops feeling like a giant
collection of features and starts feeling like a set of engineering controls you can
combine depending on the work you're doing.

title: Further learning
description: The source guide’s closing notes.

pages.text:
NEXT LEVEL
Agentic Engineering
If you're comfortable with everything in this cheat sheet, the next level isn't learning
another 100 Claude Code commands.
It's learning how to combine these ideas into a repeatable
engineering process.
That's what I go much deeper into inside my Agentic Engineering course.
The course covers how to use Claude Code and other AI coding tools across real production
applications, larger codebases, monorepos and legacy projects, including:
scoping work before
implementation
independent review Git worktrees
codebase auditing testing MCP
architecture decisions documentation hooks
feature-by-feature
development
keeping context
synchronized
parallel development
verification multiple agents production workflows

OPEN SOURCE
I've also made the underlying Agentic Engineering Skills
completely free and open source, so you can use the
workflow yourself.
The course is where I show you how all of those parts fit
together when the project becomes much bigger than
a demo.
